title: Free normal form for the Weyl-only Lie presentation
statement:
Let $I$ be a finite set and let $B=(b_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be any rational matrix. Work with rational Lie algebras and Lie ideals as in [def-wf-lie-algebra]. A free Lie algebra on a set $X$ means a rational Lie algebra with a map from $X$ such that every assignment of $X$ to a rational Lie algebra extends uniquely to a Lie homomorphism. Let $W(B)$ be the quotient of the free Lie algebra on $\{h_i,e_i,f_i:i\in I\}$ by the ideal generated by
$$[h_i,h_j],\quad [e_i,f_j]-\delta_{ij}h_i,\quad [h_i,e_j]-b_{ij}e_j,\quad [h_i,f_j]+b_{ij}f_j.$$
No Serre relations are imposed. Let $\mathcal F^-$ and $\mathcal F^+$ be free rational Lie algebras on respective symbols $y_i$ and $x_i$, and let $h^0=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbf Q u_i$ be a vector space with its indicated basis. Let $\iota_-:\mathcal F^-\to W(B)$ and $\iota_+:\mathcal F^+\to W(B)$ send $y_i$ to $f_i$ and $x_i$ to $e_i$. Then the linear map
$$\mathcal F^-\oplus h^0\oplus\mathcal F^+\longrightarrow W(B),\qquad (y,\sum_i c_i u_i,x)\longmapsto\iota_-(y)+\sum_i c_i h_i+\iota_+(x)$$
is an isomorphism of rational vector spaces. In particular both $\iota_\pm$ are injective. There are no diagonal, sign, rank or finite-type assumptions on $B$. If $I=\varnothing$, all four vector spaces are zero.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, printed p.504: the displayed Weyl-only algebra and its free negative/Cartan/free positive direct sum. The arbitrary-matrix rational form isolates the same normal-form input without using finite-type root theory. Detailed source referred to by Milne, Bourbaki, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Chapter VIII, §4, no.2, is WANTED; the agent checks this generality in report.md.

proof.text: A free Lie algebra is spanned by bracket words in its generators: the span of those words is a Lie subalgebra, the universal property gives a homomorphism into it, and its composite with inclusion is the identity by uniqueness. This also proves that $W(B)$ is generated by the displayed generators. For every $\lambda\in\mathbf Q^I$, use [lem-sfb-weyl-word-operators] to assign $h_i,e_i,f_i$ the operators $H_i,E_i,F_i$ on the word space $A(I)$. The free universal property extends this assignment to a Lie homomorphism. Its kernel is an ideal (a bracket with a kernel element maps to a bracket with zero), and contains every defining relation, so it factors through $W(B)$. Denote the resulting representation by $\rho_\lambda$. Quotient and endomorphism brackets here are those of [def-wf-lie-algebra].

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, p.504; agent construction of highest-weight word representations, with all weights allowed.

proof.text:
Suppose $\iota_-(y)+\sum_i c_i h_i+\iota_+(x)=0$. Apply $\rho_\lambda$ to the empty word. Every positive bracket word annihilates $1$, since each $E_i$ does and the bracket is the commutator. A negative bracket word acts by left multiplication by the corresponding associative commutator word. Consequently
$$q(y)+(\sum_i c_i\lambda_i)1=0\quad\text{in }A(I).$$
Here $q$ is the injective map of [lem-sfb-free-lie-word-embedding], for the generators $y_i$. Its values have zero coefficient at the empty word: each generator has positive word length, and concatenation and brackets preserve the span of nonempty words. At $\lambda=0$ the displayed equation gives $q(y)=0$, hence $y=0$. For each $j$, take $\lambda_j=1$ and all other coordinates zero; the same equation gives $c_j=0$. This uses the operator values in [lem-sfb-weyl-word-operators], not any independence assertion in $W(B)$.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, p.504; agent separation of the negative and Cartan terms by evaluation on highest-weight vectors.

proof.text: The assignment $h_i\mapsto-h_i$, $e_i\mapsto f_i$, $f_i\mapsto e_i$ respects the defining relations and therefore defines an involution $\omega$ of $W(B)$. In particular $[f_i,e_j]=-\delta_{ij}h_i=\delta_{ij}(-h_i)$, $[-h_i,f_j]=b_{ij}f_j$, and $[-h_i,e_j]=-b_{ij}e_j$; commuting Cartan generators remain commuting. Applying it twice fixes the generators, hence is the identity. If $\iota_+(x)=0$, applying $\omega$ gives $\iota_-(x^-)=0$, where $x^-$ is the image of $x$ under the free Lie isomorphism $x_i\mapsto y_i$. Step 2 gives $x^-=0$, so $x=0$. Combined with step 2 this proves injectivity of the displayed direct-sum map. The free isomorphism and the involution follow from uniqueness, and antisymmetry follows by expanding $[a+b,a+b]=0$ in [def-wf-lie-algebra].

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, p.504; elementary involution preserving the Weyl relations.

proof.text:
Put $N=\iota_-(\mathcal F^-)$, $P=\iota_+(\mathcal F^+)$, and $H=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}\{h_i\}$, without assuming their independence for the spanning argument. If $v$ is a negative bracket word with letters $f_{j_1},\ldots,f_{j_m}$, the defining relation and Jacobi give
$$[h_i,v]=-(\sum_{r=1}^m b_{i j_r})v.$$
Indeed this is a defining relation for $m=1$, and for $v=[v_1,v_2]$ the identity $[h_i,[v_1,v_2]]=[[h_i,v_1],v_2]+[v_1,[h_i,v_2]]$ adds the two coefficients. The identical induction gives the positive formula with a plus sign. Thus $[H,N]\subseteq N$, $[H,P]\subseteq P$, and $[H,H]=0$. These are direct bracket-word inductions from [def-wf-lie-algebra], not root-space assertions.

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, p.504; agent Jacobi induction on the length of same-sign bracket words.

proof.text:
For fixed $i$, induct on the length $m$ of a negative bracket word $v$. The claim is $[e_i,v]\in H$ for $m=1$, and $[e_i,v]\in N$ for $m>1$. The base is $[e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i$. For $v=[v_1,v_2]$ expand
$$[e_i,v]=[[e_i,v_1],v_2]+[v_1,[e_i,v_2]].$$
Each inner bracket belongs to $H$ if its negative word has length one, and otherwise to $N$ by induction. Since $[H,N]\subseteq N$ by step 4 and $[N,N]\subseteq N$ by definition, both terms lie in $N$. By linearity $[e_i,N]\subseteq H+N$. Apply the involution of step 3 to obtain $[f_i,P]\subseteq H+P$. Also $[e_i,H]\subseteq P$ and $[f_i,H]\subseteq N$ by the defining relations. Since $P,N$ are subalgebras, every $\operatorname{ad}(e_i)$ and $\operatorname{ad}(f_i)$ preserves $S=N+H+P$; step 4 gives the same for $\operatorname{ad}(h_i)$. The only identity used is Jacobi from [def-wf-lie-algebra].

source.place: Theorem 23.63, first proof, p.504; agent induction for the action of a simple generator on opposite-sign words.

proof.text: Let $T=\{a\in W(B):[a,S]\subseteq S\}$. Bilinearity makes $T$ a subspace, and Jacobi shows it is a Lie subalgebra: if $a,b\in T$ and $s\in S$, then $[[a,b],s]=[a,[b,s]]-[b,[a,s]]\in S$. Step 5 puts all generators in $T$, so step 1 gives $T=W(B)$. Hence $[S,S]\subseteq S$; as $S$ contains every generator, step 1 now gives $S=W(B)$. This proves surjectivity of the displayed linear map. Together with step 3 it is a linear isomorphism and its restrictions $\iota_\pm$ are injective. The subalgebra calculation uses only [def-wf-lie-algebra]. If $I=\varnothing$, a free Lie algebra on the empty set is zero by the bracket-word span argument of step 1, $h^0=0$, and $W(B)=0$. All arguments used arbitrary rational $b_{ij}$; none required a diagonal, rank, sign or finite-type condition.
